headline: High risk of prompt-injection and data leakage from AutoGen-to-ctx file/MCP handoff; shared filesystem and broad egress make the pair unsafe by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write files and run tool calls, while ctx observes Claude Code events and uses MCP/stdio plus filesystem access. That creates a plausible content bridge where AutoGen-produced files or outputs can be treated as instructions by ctx. The interaction is inferred from documented surfaces, not directly reproduced, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF AutoGen writes attacker-controlled text into a shared working directory and ctx ingests it as context or hooks output, injection is possible.
IF ctx is configured to parse file or MCP content as instructions, the risk increases.
mitigations: Use separate working directories for each agent.
Disable automatic ingestion of file contents into ctx hooks.
Add provenance tags to any AutoGen-generated artifacts.
Review and sanitize any shared MCP payloads before ctx consumes them.
requires-engineering: enforce content provenance and trust boundaries in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen explicitly handles model provider API keys and has broad network egress; ctx touches audit/runtime logs, harness records, and filesystem plus GitHub/Claude Code APIs. If they share a workspace, sensitive application data or logs can flow from one agent into the other and then out via networked APIs. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default-style setups, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same filesystem tree, file contents can be exposed across the pair.
IF ctx forwards logs or graph data to GitHub/Claude Code APIs, sensitive context may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Place each agent in a separate workspace.
Redact secrets before either agent writes logs.
Restrict ctx API access to non-sensitive projects.
Rotate any exposed model provider keys immediately.
requires-engineering: add per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGen can execute shell commands, install packages, write the filesystem, and spawn subprocesses; ctx also writes to filesystem and uses MCP/stdio with browser and API access. If both target the same directory, concurrent writes and package changes can collide and corrupt state. Because shared-state isolation is only configurable on AutoGen and not documented on ctx, the safe coordination mechanism is uncertain, so severity stays high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering or inconsistent state can occur.
IF both agents install packages into the same environment, dependency drift can break runs.
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories.
Freeze dependencies before running either agent.
Serialize package-install steps manually.
Run one agent at a time when mutating shared state.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared filesystem and environment mutations.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen can generate code, tool outputs, and other artifacts that ctx may ingest through filesystem or MCP-adjacent workflows. ctx also observes Claude Code events and can act as a harness, so it may treat upstream outputs as authoritative unless explicitly verified. That creates a realistic cascade from one agent's mistakes into the other's downstream actions, but not enough evidence for high.
conditions: IF ctx consumes AutoGen-produced artifacts without verification, errors can propagate downstream.
IF either agent uses the other's output as ground truth, incorrect actions may be taken.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before downstream actions.
Require schema validation on exchanged artifacts.
Compare outputs against an independent source before acting.
Limit ctx to observation-only mode for AutoGen runs.
requires-engineering: implement automated verification gates between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen handles model provider API keys and broad application data, while ctx touches audit/runtime logs, harness records, and graph data and calls external services such as GitHub and Claude Code. If regulated or sensitive data is present, differing logging and retention behaviors can create a compliance mismatch. The profiles do not prove a specific residency breach, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is present in the shared workflow, logs or API calls may create retention obligations.
IF the operator requires strict residency or deletion guarantees, the documented surfaces are insufficient to prove compliance.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared runs.
Disable verbose logging where possible.
Review vendor terms for GitHub and Claude Code usage.
Separate sensitive projects from ctx-managed workflows.
requires-engineering: add retention and residency controls per data class.
